Felix's onboarding interview notes are huge. what are the main takeaways

Felix Wong's notes cover 8 interviews, and these themes came up most:

1. **Unclear first step.** Six of the eight people said they weren't sure what to do after creating an account. Several clicked around the dashboard looking for a starting point.
2. **Jargon.** Terms like "workspace" and "pipeline" confused people outside ops roles. Two thought a workspace was a separate paid product.

can you explain retention curve vs churn rate in plain english, Felix keeps mixing them up in standup

Churn rate is a single number: the share of users you lose in a given period, like 6% of subscribers cancelling this month. A retention curve shows the share of a cohort still active at day 1, day 7, day 30 and so on, so you see the shape of the drop-off, not just its size. The shape is what matters. A curve that falls steeply and then flattens means you lose people early but keep a loyal core. A curve that keeps sliding means there's no stable group of users at all. Churn rate can hide this, because a blended monthly figure mixes new users, who leave fast, with long-standing ones, who rarely do. Handy line for standup: churn tells you how much you're losing, and the retention curve tells you when and who.

Say B accidentally got far more desktop traffic, and desktop converts better than mobile whatever the variant. B's overall rate then looks higher because of who saw it, not because of what it did. Within each segment, where you compare like with like, B can still be worse. First check whether the traffic split by device was roughly even across A and B. If it wasn't, the overall number is misleading, and you should either trust the segmented results or reweight to a common mix. If the split was even, something else is off, and I'd look for a tracking bug on one platform.

what's a guardrail metric? Freya mentioned it for the checkout test and I nodded like I knew

A guardrail metric is something you watch during an experiment to make sure you aren't causing harm while improving your main target. The primary metric is what you're trying to move, such as completion rate. Guardrails are things that shouldn't get worse, like page load time, error rate, support contacts, or refunds-to-purchase ratio, depending on the product. The idea is that a change can win on its target and still damage something important elsewhere. For example, a bolder prompt might lift completion while raising complaints. You usually set a threshold in advance, such as "don't ship if error rate rises more than 0.5%." Worth asking Freya which two or three guardrails she has in mind and what the limits are.
the new onboarding test looked amazing in week 1 and then flattened. Oscar says novelty effect. what's that

The novelty effect is when users react to something simply because it's new, not because it's better. People click on a changed layout out of curiosity, so the early numbers spike and then settle back as the newness wears off. The opposite exists too, called change aversion, where a good change looks bad at first because people are used to the old way. Oscar's reading fits your pattern, since the lift appeared right away and then faded. To check, compare new users, who have no old habit to break, with existing users in the same variant. If the effect holds for new users and fades for existing ones, it's novelty. For decisions, run tests long enough to see the numbers stabilise, and base the call on the later weeks, not the first one.
Rosa says our test has "SRM" and we can't trust it. wtf is SRM

SRM stands for sample ratio mismatch. It means the number of users in each variant differs from what you planned. If you set a 50/50 split and ended up with 52,000 in A and 48,000 in B, that gap is too large to be chance at that sample size. It matters because it usually signals a problem in assignment or tracking, such as a bug that drops events for one variant, or bots, or a redirect that loses some users. Those problems can bias the results in ways you can't see. So Rosa is right to flag it. The usual fix is to find the cause, correct it and rerun, instead of trying to adjust the numbers afterwards. A chi-squared test on the group sizes is the standard way to confirm the mismatch is real.

Short version: opt-in depends heavily on platform and on when you ask.

- **Android:** Before Android 13, notifications were on by default, so opt-in looked very high. Since 13, apps need a runtime permission, so Android numbers have been moving toward iOS levels.
- **Timing matters most:** Asking on first launch, before the user has seen any value, consistently does worse than asking right after a moment where a notification obviously helps, like after they follow something or set a reminder.
- **Pre-permission primers:** A custom screen explaining the benefit before the system dialog helps, mainly because it protects your one shot. On iOS, a refusal at the system prompt can only be reversed through settings.

remind me how the jobs-to-be-done switch interview works, I'm running one Thursday

The switch interview reconstructs the story of why someone changed from one solution to another. It's usually run with someone who adopted something recently, ideally within the last few months, so memory is fresh.

**Structure**
1. **First thought:** When did they first think the old way wasn't good enough? What was happening then?
2. **Passive looking:** They noticed options but weren't actively searching yet. What did they notice, and what stopped them acting?
3. **Active looking:** What did they try or compare? What did they need to believe before committing?
4. **Deciding:** What nearly stopped them? Which anxieties came up?
5. **Consuming:** How did first use go compared with what they expected?

**Forces to listen for:** the push of the current situation, the pull of the new solution, the anxiety about switching, and the habit of staying put.

**Tips:** Ask for concrete moments ("where were you, what day was it?") rather than opinions. Don't ask "why" directly. Stay on the timeline, and let silences run.
what do cancellation surveys usually tell you, and what don't they

**What they're good for**
- Spotting broad themes in stated reasons, such as "not using it enough", "missing a feature" or "switching to a competitor".
- Tracking shifts over time. If "too complicated" doubles after a release, that's a signal worth chasing.
- Finding save opportunities, for example people who say they're pausing for a season and could be offered a pause instead.

**What they don't tell you**
- **Real causes:** People give the easiest socially acceptable answer. "Too expensive" or "not using it" often hides a deeper problem, like never reaching first value.
- **Who's missing:** Only a fraction complete the survey, and they skew toward people with strong feelings.
- **Timing:** The decision usually formed weeks earlier, so the survey catches the end of the story.

**Better pairing:** Combine survey answers with behavioural data from the 30 days before cancelling, and run a handful of short follow-up calls with recent leavers. The mismatch between what people say and what they did is often the most useful finding.
in-app feedback widget vs periodic surveys, which gets better signal?

They answer different questions, so the choice depends on what you need.

**In-app widget (always available)**
- Captures feedback in context, at the moment of frustration or delight, so details are fresher.
- Skews toward bugs and complaints, since people mostly reach for it when something goes wrong.
- Gives a steady stream but not a representative sample.

**Periodic surveys (NPS, CSAT, or a custom one)**
- Reach a broader group, so you can track trends over time.
- Are less detailed and separate from the moment of use, so answers are more general.
- Suffer from survey fatigue, and response rates are usually low.

**Event-triggered micro-surveys:** A single question after a specific action, such as finishing an export, often gives the best signal for one feature because it's both in context and sampled.

**Suggestion:** Keep a lightweight widget for bugs and ideas, use a quarterly survey for trend tracking, and add micro-surveys only on the two or three flows you're actively changing. Tag everything by user segment, because an average across all users tends to hide the interesting differences.

Confluence has more structure, with spaces, page hierarchies and templates. It also integrates tightly with Jira, so it's the natural choice if you stay there. Its editing experience is clunkier, though, and clunky editing is a big reason pages go stale.

Condens is simpler and more structured, with a clear flow from raw data to nuggets to insights. Teams often find it easier to keep tidy, and it's good for sharing findings with people outside research.

zoom or google meet for our weekly all-hands? about 60 people

For now, keep your easy run short and flat, do gentle calf stretches, and use a foam roller or massage ball for a few minutes each evening. On Saturday morning, jog easily for the first 10 minutes and see how it feels. If it's sharp, pinpoint pain rather than general tightness, or if it changes how you run, cut it short and walk home. A shorter long run won't hurt your plan, but running through a calf strain could cost you a couple of weeks.

what does the taper look like for the last 2 weeks

In the second-to-last week, cut your total mileage by about 25-30% but keep the intensity. So your Wednesday session still has the same pace but fewer reps, and your long run drops to around 12-13 km. In race week, cut your volume by about half. Do two or three short easy runs of 4-5 km, with a few strides in one of them, and rest completely the day before the race. You may feel sluggish or a bit restless, and that's normal, so don't add extra runs to make up for it. Your fitness won't drop in two weeks, but tired legs will hold you back on race day.
had a cold, missed all of last week. how do I pick up again

When you restart, do two or three easy runs at about 70% of your normal volume, with no quality session. After that you can step back into the plan at the point you left it, or one week earlier if you feel flat. Don't try to cram in the missed sessions, because that's more likely to lead to injury than to help. One missed week at this stage barely affects your fitness on race day.
goal is 2:05. how should I pace race day

Aim for around 6:02 per km for the first 3 km, even though it will feel too easy, because the crowds and adrenaline will try to pull you faster. Settle into 5:55-5:56 per km from km 4 to km 16. If you feel strong at km 16, then you can pick up the pace for the last 5 km. Check your watch at each kilometre marker, and if you're more than 10 seconds off, adjust gradually rather than all at once. If you hit halfway at around 1:02:30-1:03:00, you're right on track.

It happens when the sun throws out a big burst of charged particles, called a coronal mass ejection, and it hits Earth's magnetic field. That triggers a geomagnetic storm. Normally the aurora stays near the poles, but in a strong storm the oval expands far south, so places like southern England can see it. The big one in May 2024 was rated G5, the top of the scale, and the last storm that strong was in 2003. The sun is also near the peak of its roughly 11-year activity cycle, which makes these events more likely right now. Cameras often pick up the colours better than your eyes do, which is why phone photos tend to look more vivid than the real thing.
news says uk 'avoided recession' but growth was 0.1%. what's the actual definition

The usual shorthand is two consecutive quarters of falling GDP. GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in the economy. If one quarter shrinks and the next grows, even slightly, it isn't technically a recession. So 0.1% growth means the economy is still getting bigger, just barely. Headlines can sound upbeat when the underlying picture is flat. Some economists prefer to look at GDP per person, which can be falling even while headline GDP edges up because the population is growing. So 'avoided recession' is accurate, but it doesn't mean things are going well.
antarctic sea ice record low, I thought ice was meant to be stable down there. what changed?

For decades Antarctic sea ice was fairly stable and even grew slightly, while the Arctic declined steadily. Then in 2016 it fell abruptly, and since 2023 it has hit record lows for the time of year. Scientists are still working out exactly why. One leading idea is that the ocean has been warming below the surface, so heat gets brought up and the ice melts or fails to form. Changes in winds and in the Southern Ocean's layering of salty and fresh water may also play a role. Antarctic sea ice varies a lot from year to year, so some caution is needed about reading too much into a few years. Even so, the recent drops are large enough that many researchers think a real shift may be under way, and sea ice matters because it reflects sunlight and affects ocean circulation.
why is it "estoy aburrida" but "soy aburrida" sounds wrong/different?

Some adjectives change meaning depending on whether you use ser or estar. With estar, "estoy aburrida" describes a state: you are bored right now. With ser, "soy aburrida" describes a trait: you are a boring person. So the sentence isn't wrong, it just says something quite different, and probably not what you meant.

The same pattern shows up with other adjectives:
- ser listo = to be clever; estar listo = to be ready
- ser malo = to be bad; estar malo = to be ill
- ser rico = to be wealthy; estar rico = to taste good

A rule of thumb is that ser is for identity and lasting qualities, and estar is for conditions and how things are at the moment.
preterite vs imperfect. I keep mixing them up in my notes

The preterite is for completed events, and the imperfect is for background, habits and things in progress.

Compare these:
- Ayer llamé a Lucia. (a single finished action)
- Cuando era joven, llamaba a mis amigos cada día. (a repeated habit)
- Llovía cuando salí. (it was raining, which is the scene, and then I left, which is the event)

The imperfect sets the scene and the preterite moves the story forward. Words like "ayer", "de repente" and "una vez" usually signal the preterite. Words like "siempre", "cada día" and "mientras" usually signal the imperfect. If you tell me the sentences you're unsure about, I can go through them with you.
why "el agua" but "las aguas"? and is it "el agua fría" or "fria"

"Agua" is feminine, but it starts with a stressed "a" sound. To avoid two "a" sounds running together (la agua), Spanish uses "el" in the singular. The noun is still feminine, which is why the plural goes back to "las aguas" and why adjectives stay feminine too.

So it's "el agua fría", with the feminine ending on the adjective and an accent on the í. Without the accent it would be a different word, a verb form of "freír".

The same thing happens with "el hacha" (axe) and "el águila" (eagle), and you'd say "un agua" or "una agua" depending on the speaker, though "un agua" is more common.
when do I need the "a" before a person? like "veo a Grace"

That's the personal "a", which you put before a direct object that is a specific person (or a person-like thing, such as a beloved animal).

- Veo a Grace. (I see Grace.)
- Conozco a tu jefe. (I know your boss.)
- Veo la pantalla. (no "a", because it's a thing)

It's dropped when the person is non-specific, as in "Busco un programador" (any programmer), versus "Busco a un programador que conozco" (a particular one). It's also dropped after "tener" in most uses: "Tengo dos hermanos" has no "a".

If it helps, it's close to a marker that says "this is a person receiving the action".
what's the deal with "acordarse" vs "recordar", both mean remember?

They overlap in meaning, but they work differently grammatically.

**Recordar** is a regular transitive verb, so there's no preposition:
- Recuerdo la reunión.
- No recuerdo su nombre.

**Acordarse** is reflexive and needs "de":
- Me acuerdo de la reunión.
- No me acuerdo de su nombre.

Both change their stem (recuerdo, me acuerdo). A common slip is dropping the "de" with acordarse or forgetting the "me". Recordar can also mean "to remind": "Recuérdame mañana" means "remind me tomorrow".
accents on si/sí, el/él, tu/tú, explain fast

These accents separate pairs of one-syllable words that are spelled alike but do different jobs.

- **sí** = yes (or reflexive "himself"); **si** = if
- **él** = he; **el** = the
- **tú** = you; **tu** = your
- **mí** = me (after a preposition); **mi** = my
- **té** = tea; **te** = you (object pronoun)
- **más** = more; **mas** = but (rare, literary)

Examples:
- Si tú vienes, él viene también. (If you come, he comes too.)
- Tu café es para mí. (Your coffee is for me.)

The accented form is usually the one that stands on its own as a stressed word, such as a subject pronoun or an answer, while the unaccented one is the little connecting word.

summary para from the customer interviews, does it read as insight or just a list? "Users said the dashboard was confusing. Several mentioned they couldn't find the export button. Others said the filters were hard to use. Some wanted more colours. Overall users want a simpler experience."

It's mostly a list, and the closing sentence, "users want a simpler experience," is too broad to guide any decision. The paragraph also treats all four points as equal. "More colours" is probably a preference, while not finding the export button is a task failure. Group the points by what they stop people doing, and say how many people raised each one. For example:

"Across the 12 interviews, the strongest pattern was that people couldn't complete a core task: 8 couldn't find export, and 6 abandoned filtering after their first attempt. Both point to the same cause, which is that key actions are hidden behind unlabelled icons. Requests for more colours came up twice and look like a lower priority."

I've made up the counts, so replace them with your real numbers. Naming the underlying cause is what turns the list into an insight.
customer-facing outage apology, para two. "We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused. Mistakes happen and we are doing our best to ensure it does not happen again."

This is the weakest part of the message, because it sounds like a template. "Any inconvenience this may have caused" suggests you're unsure there was a problem, and "mistakes happen" shifts the tone towards excusing it. "Doing our best" isn't a commitment. Customers who lost work or time want three things: a plain acknowledgement, a short explanation, and what you're changing. Try:

"We're sorry. For about three hours on Tuesday, you couldn't access your projects, and some of you missed deadlines because of it. The cause was a faulty database update that we failed to catch in testing. We've rolled it back and added a check that blocks changes like this before they go live."

stakeholder asks "is it significant?" about a 0.3% lift. how do I answer without sounding like a stats textbook

Split the question in two, because "significant" is carrying two meanings. Statistical significance asks whether the lift is likely to be real rather than noise. Something like: "The result looks real, with a p-value of X, but the lift is small, so the question is whether 0.3% justifies the maintenance and rollout effort." why does Hugo keep insisting on cohort analysis instead of just looking at the overall weekly numbers

Overall weekly numbers blend together users who joined at different times and behave differently. If you're growing fast, the total can look healthy simply because a flood of new users is masking older ones drifting away. A cohort analysis groups users by when they joined, say everyone who signed up in March, and follows each group over time. You can then see whether newer cohorts retain better or worse than older ones, which tells you whether product changes are helping. It also separates a real improvement from a bump caused by a marketing push. Aggregates answer "how are we doing right now", while cohorts answer "are we getting better at keeping people". explain funnel conversion vs step drop-off, Malik's chart has both and I can't tell which to focus on

Overall funnel conversion is the share of people who enter at step one and make it all the way to the end. Step drop-off is the share lost between two consecutive steps. The first tells you how well the whole journey performs, and the second tells you where it's leaking. A step losing 60% of a small group matters less than one losing 25% of a huge group. Then ask how fixable the drop-off is. quick digest on onboarding checklists and activation? want something to read out at standup

Here's a standup-sized version.

- **What the research says:** Checklists tend to lift activation when they point to one clear first-value action. They work through the goal-gradient effect, because people push harder as they see progress, and through the Zeigarnik effect, because unfinished items nag at us.
- **Where they backfire:** Long lists (more than about five to seven items) read as homework. Lists that mix "set up your profile" with real value steps also drag completion down, because users tick the easy items and never reach the useful one.
- **What seems to work:** Pre-tick one step so the bar starts above zero. Make the first item achievable in under two minutes. Let people dismiss the list and bring it back later.
- **Measurement caveat:** Checklist completion is a vanity metric unless it's tied to a downstream event, such as a second-week return visit.

The case studies behind these points mostly come from vendor blogs, so I'd call them directional rather than proven. If you want, I can suggest an A/B test that separates "checklist present" from "first step pre-ticked".

digest on search autocomplete, what actually matters

These are the main points from the usability research I know of, mostly from Baymard and similar studies.

- **Speed and stability:** Suggestions should appear fast and not jump around while the user types. Flickering lists hurt trust more than a slightly slower one.
- **Suggestion quality over quantity:** Around eight to ten suggestions on desktop and fewer on mobile is a common range. Past that, people stop scanning.
- **Match highlighting:** Bolding the part the user hasn't typed yet is easier to scan than bolding what they've typed.
- **Scoped suggestions:** If your product has distinct areas (people, documents, settings), grouping suggestions by type helps, but only if the groups are few.
- **Typo tolerance:** Autocomplete that fails on a single misspelling feels broken.
- **Keyboard support:** Arrow keys, Enter and Escape should all behave as expected, and screen readers need the combobox pattern implemented correctly.
- **Zero-state:** Recent searches shown on focus often help more than trending suggestions.

I can sketch metrics to track, such as suggestion click-through and searches with no results.

empty states. what's the evidence they matter, or is it just design folk being precious

There's some real evidence, though less than the amount of enthusiasm suggests.

**What supports them:** An empty screen is often a user's first impression of a feature, and it's where people decide whether to continue. Usability studies and practitioner case studies consistently find that empty states which explain the purpose and offer one clear next action beat blank screens or generic "No data" messages. They also cut support questions like "is it broken?".

**Caveats:** Most published results are from case studies without rigorous controls, so the effect sizes are uncertain. The effect is also likely biggest where the empty state is hit by most new users, such as a first project or first report, and small for screens only seen occasionally.

**Practical approach:** Look for the three or four screens new users hit empty most often, rewrite those with a purpose line, a primary action and perhaps sample content, and compare first-week activation before and after. That would tell you more than the literature will.

**Where they struggle**

product-led vs sales-led for B2B SaaS, two minute read for Imogen

**Product-led growth (PLG):** The product itself acquires and converts users, usually through a free tier or trial where people experience value before talking to anyone. It scales cheaply, spreads bottom-up inside companies, and gives you rich usage data. The weaknesses are that it needs a product people can understand and use unaided, and large buyers may still want a human to speak to.

**Sales-led:** Reps lead discovery, demos and onboarding. It suits complex, high-stakes products with many stakeholders, and it gives you close contact with customers. It's slower and costlier to scale, and it can hide product friction because a person smooths it over.

**What most companies do:** Run a hybrid. Individual users or small teams self-serve, and when usage signals show an account growing (more seats, more teams, admin features requested), sales steps in. This is often called product-led sales.

**Questions to decide for us:**
1. How quickly can a new user reach value without help?
2. Who makes the buying decision, and how many people are involved?
3. Do we have usage signals reliable enough to tell sales where to focus?

If Imogen wants more depth, the third question is the best place to dig.

- Es para ti. (it's for you)

hay vs está/están, I always pick wrong

- El informe está en la carpeta. (The report, which we both know about, is in the folder.)
- Hay tres opciones. / Las opciones están abajo.

"Hay" never changes for plural, so it's "hay una persona" and "hay muchas personas". The past version is "había" (imperfect) or "hubo" (preterite).

- The "if" clause uses the imperfect subjunctive: si tuviera tiempo.
- The result clause uses the conditional: iría.

The imperfect subjunctive is built from the third-person plural preterite. Take tuvieron, drop "-ron" and add -ra endings: tuviera, tuvieras, tuviera, tuviéramos, tuvieran. The conditional is the infinitive plus endings: ir + ía = iría.

One firm rule is that you never put the conditional in the "si" clause. "Si tendría tiempo" is a common learner error.

In most of Spain, the present perfect ("he comido") is used for anything in a period that includes the present: "Hoy he comido temprano", "Esta semana he trabajado mucho". The preterite ("comí") is for finished time periods: "Ayer comí temprano".

In much of Latin America, speakers often use the preterite for both, so "Hoy comí temprano" sounds perfectly natural. The present perfect is used there too, but more for experiences and results connected with now, such as "Nunca he estado allí".

If you're mostly talking with people in Spain, the "hoy/esta semana + he..." pattern is a safe default.

- Hazlo. (Do it.) and No lo hagas. (Don't do it.)
- Envíamelo. (Send it to me.) and No me lo envíes. (Don't send it to me.)

The verb form changes too. The affirmative tú command is usually the same as the he/she present form (habla, come), while the negative uses the subjunctive (no hables, no comas). That's why "di" becomes "digas".

When you stack pronouns, the order is always indirect before direct, as in "me lo", and attached ones may need a written accent to keep the stress, as in "envíamelo".

- Hace + time + que + present: Hace dos años que trabajo aquí.

If the water is still slow after all that, the blockage is probably further down the pipe, and that's the point to call a plumber.
how do i share my calendar with Felix so he only sees when I'm busy, not what the meetings are

Assuming Google Calendar, on a computer, hover over your calendar name in the left sidebar, click the three dots, then Settings and sharing. Scroll to Share with specific people or groups and click Add people. Enter Felix's email address. In the Permissions dropdown, choose See only free/busy (hide details), then click Send. He'll get an email invite, and from then on he'll see blocks of time marked busy without titles or attendees. If you're on Outlook instead, right-click your calendar, choose Share, add Felix, and set the permission to Can view when I'm busy. Let me know which one you're on and I can adjust the steps.
black mould along the sealant round the bath. how do i get rid of it

Start by ventilating the room and wearing rubber gloves. Spray the mouldy sealant with a mould remover, or a mix of white vinegar and water if you prefer something gentler, and leave it for 15 to 30 minutes. Scrub with an old toothbrush, rinse, and dry thoroughly with a cloth. If the black staining goes deep into the sealant and doesn't shift, the mould has got in behind the surface. In that case you'll need to cut out the old sealant with a sealant remover tool or a sharp scraper, let the gap dry completely, and apply fresh silicone sealant made for bathrooms. To keep it from coming back, run the extractor fan or open a window for 20 minutes after each shower, and wipe down wet surfaces.
got a ton of duplicate contacts on my phone, easy way to merge them?

On an iPhone running iOS 16 or later, open the Contacts app (or the Phone app and tap Contacts), then tap Lists in the top-left corner. If your phone has found duplicates, you'll see a Duplicates Found banner at the top of the list. Tap it, then choose Merge All, or review them one at a time with Merge. It's worth glancing through before merging everything, in case two different people share a name. On Android, open Google Contacts, tap Suggestions at the bottom, then Merge & fix, and choose Merge duplicates. Before you start, it's a good idea to make sure your contacts are backed up, just in case.
power just tripped and the kitchen sockets are dead

Check your fuse box (consumer unit), which is usually near the front door or under the stairs. Look for any switch that's flipped down or sitting differently from the others. Before resetting it, unplug whatever was running in the kitchen when it went, as a faulty appliance is the most common culprit. Then push the tripped switch firmly back up. If the main RCD switch has tripped, you may need to reset the individual circuit switches afterwards too. Plug appliances back in one at a time so you can spot which one causes trouble. Don't open the fuse box cover or touch anything inside it, and keep your hands dry.
it tripped again straight away

Then leave it off for now. Unplug everything on that kitchen circuit, including things like the fridge and kettle, and try the switch once more. If it still trips with nothing plugged in, the problem is in the wiring or a fixed appliance like the oven or dishwasher, so you'll need an electrician. If it holds, plug devices back in one by one and the one that trips it is faulty. In the meantime, keep the fridge door shut so the food stays cold.
my earbuds keep connecting to my phone instead of my laptop. how do i make them switch properly

Bluetooth earbuds usually hold onto whichever device they connected to last, so a manual switch is the most reliable fix. Turn off Bluetooth on your phone (or tap the earbuds' name in its Bluetooth settings and choose Disconnect), then select the earbuds in your laptop's Bluetooth menu. If you have AirPods and a Mac, set the phone's Connect to This iPhone option under the AirPods settings to When Last Connected to This iPhone, which stops it grabbing them automatically. Some other brands have a multipoint setting in their companion app that lets them stay paired to two devices at once, so check yours. If it still misbehaves, remove the earbuds from both devices and re-pair them to the laptop first, then the phone.
dishwasher smells a bit funky, what do i do

It's almost always trapped food and grease. Start with the filter: pull out the bottom rack, twist out the filter at the base, and rinse it under the tap, scrubbing gently with an old toothbrush. Wipe around the door seal and the spray arms too, since gunk collects there. Then run a cleaning cycle. Put a cup of white vinegar upright on the top rack of the empty machine and run the hottest wash. Or sprinkle a cup of bicarbonate of soda across the bottom and do a short hot rinse afterwards. Leaving the door slightly ajar between uses will help it dry out, which stops the smell coming back.
feature name for saved searches. engineering calls it "query persistence" 🙄

Users don't think in queries, so the name should describe what they get. Some options:

- Bookmarks, which is familiar but may be confused with browser bookmarks.
- Saved Views, which is clear and works if filters are part of what's saved.
- Shortcuts, which is friendly but vague.
- Pinned Searches, which is specific and suggests they stay put.
- Watchlists, which fits if you later add alerts when new results appear.

I'd go with Saved Views if the feature stores filters and sorting as well as the search text. If you plan to add notifications, Watchlists leaves more room to grow. "Query persistence" can stay as the ticket title and nowhere else.
name for our customer research panel? Grace is recruiting and needs something for the invite page

The name should make people feel like insiders rather than test subjects. Some options:

- The Sounding Board
- Inside Track
- Workbench Circle
- Field Notes Club
- The Advisory Bench
- Open Door

I'd pick Sounding Board for the invite page. It tells people what they're being asked to do, which is give honest reactions, and it carries no jargon. Open Door is warmer but could sound like a general feedback inbox. Whichever you choose, Grace could add a one-line promise under it, such as "Help shape what we build next, about 30 minutes a month." That's what makes people actually sign up.
beta programme needs a name that doesn't sound like a hospital trial

Fair point, "Beta Cohort 1" does sound clinical. Try names that suggest early access and a bit of privilege:

- Early Light
- First Look
- Preview Crew
- The Pilot Seat Club
- Trailblazers (a bit overused)
- Lab Pass
- Sneak Peek

My top two are First Look and Early Light. First Look is self-explanatory, so nobody needs a glossary. Early Light is more distinctive and fits if the product has any sunrise or brightness in its branding. I'd avoid Trailblazers because several other companies use it and people may think it's copied.
Slack channel name for the platform migration? Dmitri's team want something fun but findable

A channel needs a searchable prefix so people can find it, with a bit of personality after it. Here are some ideas:

- #migration-moving-day
- #migration-lift-and-shift
- #migration-the-big-move
- #migration-no-going-back
- #migration-bridge-building

I'd use #migration-moving-day. It sorts with any other migration channels, it's clear to someone who's just joined, and it has a light tone for what will probably be a long project. If Dmitri's team prefers something shorter, #migration-bridge works and gives you a theme for milestone names later, like Tower, Waterloo and Westminster.
ha, bridge milestones. go on

Here's a sequence in rough order of scale. Start with Putney for the smallest pilot move, then Hammersmith for the first real team, Waterloo for the bulk of the data, Westminster for the high-visibility services, and Tower Bridge for the final cutover. Each name has a visual people can picture. Just check the order sounds like a journey and not a random list.
how else can we get early feedback on the new search besides interviews? Kwame says interviews are too slow

There are several faster ways, and they work best in combination.

1. A one-question prompt inside the product after someone uses search, such as "Did you find what you wanted?" with a yes/no and an optional comment.
2. A short window of watching anonymised session recordings, focused on searches that end with no click.
3. A shared doc where support and sales log search complaints they hear, with a weekly review.
4. A small group of power users who get early access and a direct channel to the team.
5. A "zero results" report, which shows the queries where search fails completely.

I'd start with the zero results report and the in-product prompt. Both run continuously, need little effort from users, and give Kwame something concrete to look at within a week.
what should we call the retro format where we look at what we'd do differently, trying to avoid "retro"

Some alternatives, depending on how formal you want it:

- Look Back, Look Ahead
- Rewind
- The Debrief
- Keep, Drop, Try (describes the structure itself)
- Post-Project Pause
- Second Draft

I like Second Draft. It frames the session as improving the next version rather than assigning blame, which helps people speak openly. Keep, Drop, Try is the most practical because the name doubles as the agenda: three columns, and everyone knows what to bring. You could use Second Draft as the name and Keep, Drop, Try as the format.
Lucia wants a theme for naming our quarterly releases. not letters or numbers. thoughts?

Release themes work best when the set is large, easy to order and not too serious. Some options:

- London bridges, such as Putney, Kew, Chelsea and Waterloo. There are enough, and a rough order exists.
- Rivers, from the Thames to the Fleet, with room to include lost rivers.
- Trees, like Alder, Birch, Cedar and Elm, which also sort alphabetically so the order is obvious.
- Cheeses, which are memorable but harder to explain externally.
- Weather terms, like Drizzle and Squall, which fit a British team's sense of humour.

I'd suggest trees. They run alphabetically, there are plenty of them, and nobody will argue about the sequence. If Lucia wants a stronger local identity, the lost rivers of London give you a good story and a few unusual names.

can you look at this release note para? "We're excited to announce that we have now rolled out a brand new notifications experience which has been completely redesigned to give users more control over what they receive and when they receive it, and we hope you will find it useful."

The content is fine, but it's one long sentence and the useful part is buried. "Excited to announce" and "we hope you find it useful" are filler, and "brand new" and "completely redesigned" say the same thing twice. The reader wants to know what they can now do. Here's a tighter version:

"Notifications are now yours to control. You can choose which alerts you get, set quiet hours, and switch between instant and daily digest delivery, all from Settings > Notifications."

It's about half the length and gives people a concrete next step. If you want to keep some warmth, a short closing line like "Tell us what you'd change" works better than "we hope you find it useful."

opening para of the Q3 strategy doc, does it grab you? "This document outlines our product strategy for Q3. It covers our goals, the key initiatives we will pursue, and the metrics we will use to measure success. It is intended to align the team and stakeholders."

Honestly, no. It describes the document rather than the strategy, and any strategy doc could open with those three sentences. People will skim it and miss the point. Lead with the bet you're making and why it matters now. Something like:

"In Q3 we're focusing on getting new teams to their first successful project within a week. Activation is where we lose the most people, and it's the cheapest place to improve retention. Everything below, from the goals to the initiatives to the metrics, follows from that choice."

I've guessed at the specifics, so swap in your real focus. Keep the last sentence, because it tells readers how the rest of the doc fits together.

linkedin about section, be blunt: "I'm a passionate product manager with 8 years of experience building products that users love. I'm a team player who thrives in fast-paced environments and loves solving complex problems."

Blunt version: it could be anyone's. "Passionate," "team player," "thrives in fast-paced environments" and "products users love" are the most common phrases in PM profiles, so they don't help you stand out. Eight years is a good fact, but it needs something concrete beside it. Say what kinds of products you've built, for whom, and one result you're proud of. Cut the adjectives about yourself and let the details show it. A skeleton would be:

"I'm a product manager with eight years in [sector], most recently leading [product] for [type of user]. I'm best when a problem is messy and nobody agrees what it is yet. Recent work includes [specific outcome]."

Give me two or three real outcomes and I'll draft the full thing.
ok one: cut support tickets about onboarding by a third
That's a good one. Try: "Recently I led a rework of onboarding that cut related support tickets by a third." Put it right after the opening line so it's the first proof a reader sees.

email to Kwame about the slipped roadmap item. is this clear? "Unfortunately the export feature is going to be a bit delayed due to some unforeseen technical challenges. We're working hard to resolve them and will keep you updated."

It's polite, but Kwame will have follow-up questions straight away, which means he'll need another email from you. "A bit delayed" doesn't say how long, "unforeseen technical challenges" doesn't say what, and "will keep you updated" doesn't say when. People tolerate slips much better when they get a new date and a reason they can repeat to others. A stronger version:

"Kwame, the export feature will slip from the 12th to the week of the 26th. The data format we planned to use can't handle large accounts, so the team is switching to a different approach. I'll confirm the new date by Thursday once they've finished testing it."

Adjust the dates and the reason to match reality. If any of it is still uncertain, say that explicitly and give the day you'll know.

job ad para for the senior designer role, thoughts? "We are looking for a rockstar designer who can hit the ground running and wear many hats. You must be able to work independently and handle a high-pressure environment."

I'd rewrite it. "Rockstar," "hit the ground running," and "wear many hats" are the phrases that put off thoughtful senior candidates, because they tend to mean overworked and unclear scope. "High-pressure environment" is a warning sign unless you explain it. The paragraph also describes only what you want from them and says nothing about what the role offers. Try something like:

"You'll be the senior designer embedded in our product team, owning the experience from early discovery through to launch. You'll work closely with product and engineering, and you'll have real say in what we build and why. We're a small team with deadlines, so we'd like someone who is comfortable making decisions with incomplete information and asking for help when it matters."

That is still honest about the pace, but it reads as an invitation instead of a warning.
blog intro, feels flat. "Onboarding is an important part of any product. In this post I'm going to talk about some lessons we learned when we redesigned ours, and hopefully you'll find them helpful."

Flat is right. Both sentences promise a post rather than starting it, and "onboarding is an important part of any product" is something every reader already agrees with. A good intro gives the reader a reason to keep going within a line or two. Start with the most surprising thing you learned, or with the moment that showed the old flow was failing. For example:

"Our old onboarding had a 40% drop-off at step two, and we spent a month fixing the wrong thing. Here's what we got wrong, and what finally worked."

Use your own story and numbers, of course. Admitting a mistake early makes readers trust you, and "hopefully you'll find them helpful" can go entirely.

writing a promo case for Zoe. this para ok? "Zoe has consistently exceeded expectations this year and is a great collaborator. She deserves to be promoted to senior analyst because she works very hard and is liked by everyone."

It's warm, but it's the kind of case a review panel can't use. "Exceeded expectations," "great collaborator" and "works very hard" are claims without evidence, and "liked by everyone" isn't a promotion criterion. The panel is asking whether Zoe is already working at the next level, so you need to show that. Pick two or three pieces of work, say what she did, and say what changed because of it. A structure that works:

"Zoe is already operating at senior analyst level. This year she [led X without direction], which [result]. She also [mentored or unblocked someone], so [effect on the team]. Her work on [Y] changed how we decide [Z]."

Send me the actual examples and I'll turn this into finished prose.
problem statement for the PRD: "Users have a hard time managing their projects and we need to improve the experience so that they are more productive and satisfied."

This is too general to be tested. "Managing their projects" covers a huge area, and "more productive and satisfied" can't be measured, so the team could build almost anything and say it solved the problem. A good problem statement names who is affected, what they're trying to do, what gets in the way, and how you'll know it's fixed. For example:

"Team leads who run more than five concurrent projects can't see which ones are at risk without opening each one. They spend about 30 minutes a day checking manually, and they often learn about slipping work too late to act. Success means leads can identify at-risk projects in under a minute from one view."

The numbers are placeholders, so fill them in from your research. Even rough figures make the statement far easier to design and test against.
do I need the 30 mins if I don't have data

No, don't include a figure you can't back up. Say "a significant amount of time, according to interviews" or leave it out, and add a line in the doc saying you'll validate it. An honest gap is better than a number someone later asks you to source.

slack post announcing we're changing retros. too stiff? "Please be advised that effective next sprint, retrospectives will be held biweekly instead of weekly. Attendance is expected. Kindly review the new format in the linked doc beforehand."

A bit, yes. "Please be advised," "effective," and "kindly" sound like a notice from HR, and "attendance is expected" will make people defensive about a change that is meant to give them time back. It also doesn't say why you're changing it, which is what people will want to know. A friendlier version:

"Quick change to retros: from next sprint we'll run them every two weeks instead of every week. Weekly ones were getting repetitive, so we'll use the longer gap to go deeper on what actually matters. There's a short doc with the new format here, and it would help if you skimmed it before the first one. Shout if you have concerns!"

It keeps the practical details and sounds like you.

bio for the team wiki, bit long maybe? "Maya Brooks is a product manager based in London who has worked in tech for many years across a variety of companies and industries. She enjoys working with cross-functional teams to deliver impactful products and is always looking for ways to learn and grow. Outside of work she likes reading and walking."

The length is fine for a wiki, but the content is generic, so it could shorten and still say the same. "Many years," "a variety of companies," "impactful products," and "always looking to learn and grow" don't tell colleagues anything they can use. A team wiki bio is mostly there to help people know what to come to you for. Try:

"Maya Brooks is a product manager in London, currently leading [area]. Come to her for help with [e.g. untangling unclear requirements, planning a roadmap, or turning research into decisions]. Before this she worked on [one or two products]. Outside work she reads a lot and walks whenever the weather allows."

Fill in the brackets. I'd keep the reading and walking line, since it's the only part that sounds like a person.
